items.title: [abc.net.au] Lancet researchers urge health emergency declaration as climate losses mount
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Heat-related disruption cost the world an estimated $1.07 trillion in lost worker productivity in 2025, while extreme drought affected about 52% of global land for at least a month, according to the 2026 Lancet Countdown report. The report’s 146 researchers from 30 countries urged governments to treat climate change as a global health emergency and coordinate a sustained response. Extreme rainfall affected 17.2% of global land each year from 2016 to 2025, up from 14.8% in the preceding decade, and the researchers linked shifting groundwater conditions to risks for food security and sanitation. Southeast Asia and Africa suffered the largest productivity-related economic losses, equivalent to 3.9% and 3.2% of gross domestic product, respectively. Clean-energy investment reached $2.1 trillion in 2025, nearly twice fossil-fuel investment, but fossil fuels still supplied more than 80% of global energy. The report calls for governments to consider health in climate decisions and direct climate and health funding to vulnerable countries. Researchers are expected to press the issue at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye, scheduled for Nov. 9-20.

items.title: [theguardian.com] UN warns climate adaptation funding leaves vulnerable countries exposed
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

A United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) report says developing countries remain exposed to worsening floods, droughts and heat because adaptation funding is not reaching vulnerable communities at the scale required. Least-developed countries and small island states need an estimated $40 billion to $50 billion annually, equivalent to 3% to 4% of their gross domestic product, while support to least-developed countries fell 16% from 2022 to 2024. Adaptation measures include flood barriers, heat-resistant hospitals and drought-resilient water and farming systems. Low- and middle-income countries accounted for 99% of the 765 million people affected by floods and landslides between 2020 and 2025. Communities also face obstacles to turning plans into projects, including weak institutional coordination and difficulty accessing funding for climate-related losses. At the COP31 climate conference, opening in Antalya on Nov. 9, campaigners are urging governments to set out a concrete funding plan and prioritize grants or concessional loans over high-interest borrowing for projects that generate little direct revenue. Concessional loans are easier to repay than high-interest loans.

items.title: [news.un.org] UN says record greenhouse gases lock in centuries-long warming
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO), the United Nations’ weather agency, reported that atmospheric concentrations of carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide all reached record levels in 2025. Carbon dioxide averaged 426.8 parts per million, methane 1,948 parts per billion and nitrous oxide 339.1 parts per billion—153%, 267% and 126% of pre-industrial levels, respectively. The annual bulletin measures gases accumulated in the atmosphere, not emissions released during the year. About half of annual carbon dioxide emissions remain in the atmosphere. The WMO says the gases’ heat-trapping effect will drive warming for decades or centuries; the past 11 years were the warmest on record. Carbon dioxide rose 2.8 parts per million from 2024 to 2025, below the previous year’s 3.6-ppm increase but still above the decade average of 2.6 ppm. The WMO linked the slower increase partly to recovering land carbon sinks and fewer fire emissions after the 2023-24 El Niño. It warned that concentrations could rise further in 2026 as fossil-fuel use continues and another powerful El Niño affects land sinks. The bulletin will inform negotiators at the Nov. 9-20 COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye.

items.title: [LoRaMeshDevices] DIY Meshtastic Solar Node: Muziworks Uno Full Build Guide
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

A bare Meshtastic board, a battery and a solar panel are a good start. To turn them into something I can leave outside, I want a proper enclosure, a secure mounting arrangement, an external antenna and sealed cable entries. For this build, I’m using the Elecrow Muziworks Muzi Base Uno. I already had the small solar panel wired up and the basic configuration working. Now I’m putting everything into a weatherproof case, updating the firmware and getting the node ready for an outdoor test. The big question is the solar panel. It is very small, and I’m not yet convinced it will keep the battery charged. This is a working build ready for testing, not a proven, indefinitely self-sufficient solar installation. Key Takeaways Update and verify the firmware before enclosing the board, while USB access is easy. Plan the internal layout around USB clearance, battery-connector access and safe assembly. Seal every new enclosure opening, including the solar-wire entry behind the panel. Successful mesh communication does not prove the small solar panel can sustain the node. Table of Contents Parts and Layout Update the Meshtastic Firmware First Make a Small 3D-Printed Board Mount Prepare the Enclosure and External Connections Mount the Board and Battery Route, Solder and Attach the Solar Panel Seal the Cable Entry and Check the Finished Layout Configure the Node for a Fixed Installation Run a Traceroute Before Mounting Outside Put It Outside and Test the Solar Side Parts and Layout The Uno does not have the Wi-Fi capability of the Duo, which suits what I want from this solar node. It also came with a small three-wire battery, including a sensing wire rather than just the usual positive and negative connections. Here is what I used: Muzi Base Uno and its supplied battery. A weatherproof enclosure with rear mounting hardware and an internal mounting plate. A small solar panel, already connected during the earlier setup. An SMA male to N female bulkhead adapter for the external antenna connection. A larger 915 MHz external antenna. A gasketed enclosure breather plug. A custom 3D-printed board mount, small screws, 3M double-sided mounting tape and silicone sealant. The linked parts are affiliate links, which means I may earn from qualifying purchases. Before fixing anything down, check the whole layout. The board needs room for its antenna connection, battery plug and solar wiring. Just as importantly, leave enough clearance to connect a USB cable for future firmware updates. A neat installation is not much use if you have to dismantle it every time you need access. Update the Meshtastic Firmware First I did the firmware update before putting the board in the enclosure. It is much easier to work with the USB connection while everything is still on the bench. Connect the antenna before powering the board. I kept that same order later when connecting the battery. Connect the Uno to the computer with a USB cable. Open the Meshtastic web flasher at flasher.meshtastic.org. Select Muziworks, then the Muzi Base Uno/Duo device entry. Select the firmware version and start the flashing process. Follow the prompt to put the nRF-based board into DFU mode. When the board appears as a removable drive, download the matching UF2 firmware file. Copy the UF2 file onto that drive and wait for the transfer to finish. I chose Meshtastic 2.8.2 alpha for this build. That was a deliberate choice to try the newer firmware, not a recommendation to treat an alpha release as stable. The flasher offered different release channels, so check what you are selecting rather than simply assuming the newest option is the best one. Before copying the new firmware over, I also saved a copy of the existing UF2 file from the device drive to my computer. That gave me a local copy of the old firmware. I would not treat that as a separate backup of all the device settings. Once the copy completed, the drive ejected and disappeared as the board restarted. I reconnected in the Meshtastic app and checked the device details. The firmware version now showed 2.8.2, which confirmed the update had worked. Take an Initial Noise Reading The newer firmware exposed an antenna noise reading that I wanted to try. With the little stock antenna attached, the app reported approximately -97 dBm and displayed the result in green. That gave me a useful starting point before changing the enclosure and antenna. It is a noise-floor reading, though, not a range test or a measurement of antenna gain. For noise, a more negative value means a lower noise level: -97 dBm is quieter than -83 dBm. Make a Small 3D-Printed Board Mount I like mounting the board on a small raised plate rather than fixing it directly against the bottom of the enclosure. It keeps the installation tidier and leaves some space underneath the components. For this one, I drew a basic sketch with the dimensions I needed and used AI to help turn it into a printable mount. The result was an STL file that I opened in the slicer, checked and printed in PETG. The mounting-hole spacing came out correctly, and the board fitted the printed part. I used three small screws to secure it. The printed mount is optional. What matters is keeping the board secure, clear of the enclosure floor and accessible enough to maintain. There was one detail I would improve in another version: make the battery connector easier to reach after the board is mounted. That became awkward during assembly. Prepare the Enclosure and External Connections I have used this style of enclosure on other outdoor nodes without problems, so it is a familiar starting point. The supplied brackets attach to the back for mounting against a wall or another support. The case also came with cable-entry fittings, but I did not need those for this layout. Instead, I made openings for: The antenna bulkhead at the top. The breather plug on the side. The solar-panel wires behind the panel. I drilled the antenna and breather openings first. The solar-wire hole came later in my assembly, although planning all the openings before installing the electronics would make the job simpler. Fit the Breather Plug The breather plug is there to help manage moisture inside the enclosure. I am not using it as a cooling vent. It passes through the side wall and tightens against a rubber gasket. I seated the gasket against the case and tightened the fitting so it sat securely. Fit the Antenna Bulkhead The antenna connection uses an SMA male to N female bulkhead arrangement. Check the actual connector contacts as well as the threads: in this build, the SMA pin mates with the socket on the board’s antenna connection. The bulkhead passes through the top of the enclosure and has its own rubber gasket. Tightening the retaining hardware compresses that gasket against the case. The antenna and breather fittings are in place before the electronics go into the case. I then fitted the larger 915 MHz antenna to the outside. The N connector gives me a substantial external connection rather than leaving the small board-level connection exposed. Mount the Board and Battery With the external fittings installed, I checked the internal layout again. I positioned the printed mount low enough in the case to preserve USB access, with the battery beside it and room to route the antenna and solar wiring. I used two strips of 3M double-sided tape beneath the printed mount. I have had good results with this tape on other outdoor builds, so I used it again for the mount, battery and panel. Getting the backing off the tape is usually the part that tests my patience. This time, it was not too bad. The more important difficulty was the battery connector. I initially had the board attached to the mount, then removed it again because I was bending the cable and making the assembly awkward to handle. With the mount fixed down, I connected the antenna, plugged in the battery and taped the battery into the middle of the case. Everything fitted, but reinstalling the board screws while it was powered made me uncomfortable. A dropped screw could short the board. That is the part of this assembly I would change: finish the screw work with power disconnected. A better connector-access cutout in the mount, or a suitable power switch, would make the build much easier to work on. There is no prize for trying to balance tiny screws over a live board. Route, Solder and Attach the Solar Panel The panel sits on the outside of the lid. To get its wires through the enclosure, I disconnected the panel leads, drilled a small hole behind its intended position and passed the wires through. I then soldered the leads back onto the panel, keeping positive and negative on their correct connections. Check the panel position against the lid. Route the wires through the opening behind the panel. Reconnect the positive and negative leads. Check that the wires and solder joints do not prevent the panel from sitting properly. Attach the panel with mounting tape. Seal the wire opening with silicone. I ran into a small problem here: the solder connection on the back of the panel stood proud enough to stop it sitting flat against the lid. The first two strips of tape did not provide enough clearance. I adjusted the mounting with additional tape so the panel could sit properly without rocking on the solder joint. It is worth checking that clearance before pressing the adhesive down firmly. The panel’s rating was not clearly established during this build, so I am not going to give it a definite wattage or current specification. It is simply a very small panel, and its ability to keep this node running still needs an outdoor test. Seal the Cable Entry and Check the Finished Layout The antenna bulkhead and breather plug have gaskets, but the solar-wire hole needs separate sealing. I used silicone around that opening to keep water from entering along the wires. The hole is behind the solar panel, which gives it some shelter, but that is not a substitute for sealing it. Before closing the lid, I checked the main items: The board and battery were secured. The antenna connection was attached. The solar leads were connected and routed inside the case. The USB port remained accessible. The external fittings were tightened and the wire entry was sealed. At this point, the node was assembled in an enclosure intended for outdoor use. That is different from having a verified waterproof rating for the modified build. The drilled openings and seals still need to hold up in practice. Configure the Node for a Fixed Installation Back in the Meshtastic app, I requested another noise reading with the external antenna connected. It returned approximately -97 dBm, much like the stock antenna reading on the bench. That was encouraging, but it did not demonstrate a range improvement. The node was still indoors, and a noise reading alone cannot tell me how well a rooftop installation will perform. I initially left the device in Client mode. For this fixed-node experiment, I then changed the role to Client Base, selected the option to rebroadcast everything and saved the settings. The node restarted and reappeared in the app. Those are the settings I chose for this installation, rather than a claim that every solar-powered Meshtastic node should use exactly the same configuration. Run a Traceroute Before Mounting Outside For a basic connectivity check, I tried a traceroute to a nearby node down the street. The request reached it directly, while the reply came back through a different path. That confirmed the assembled node could communicate on the mesh. I then stood the enclosure upright so the antenna was vertical instead of lying along the desk and repeated the test. The displayed link reading improved from roughly -11 dB to -9 dB. It was a useful reminder to test the antenna in its intended orientation, but it was still only a short bench check, not a measured outdoor range test. Put It Outside and Test the Solar Side For the first outdoor trial, I mounted the enclosure on the side of my garden shed. This is not its final position. I wanted an accessible place to see whether the whole assembly worked before moving it to a roof. The shed mount is a temporary test position before a possible roof installation. By then, the solar-panel mounting had been sorted out, the case was closed and the node was running. Firmware flashing, the external antenna connection and the initial mesh checks had all worked. The unresolved part is the energy budget. I need to leave it outside over the next few days and find out whether that little panel can keep up with the node’s consumption. For now, I have a tidy, enclosed Meshtastic solar-node build ready for that test. If the panel proves too small, that will be the next thing to change. Getting the hardware assembled is one milestone; proving that it can stay running outside is the next one.

items.title: [space.com] ISS astronauts install seventh upgraded solar array during 100th US spacewalk
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

NASA astronaut Anil Menon and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk installed and unfurled the International Space Station’s seventh upgraded roll-out solar array on Oct. 29, completing a 7-hour, 11-minute spacewalk that marked the 100th U.S. spacewalk from the station. The new panel adds about 8 kilowatts of power to support station operations as the original arrays lose output after exceeding their 15-year design life. The crew used the Canadarm2 robotic arm to move the array to its mounting point and connected it to power channel 2A. The new arrays supplement, rather than replace, the station’s original solar wings; together, they are expected to raise available power to about 215 kilowatts. The extra capacity will support research, life-support systems and visiting spacecraft through the station’s planned 2030 retirement and controlled deorbit. The crew also completed preparatory work for the eighth and final array. Menon and Kutryk are scheduled to install it on Nov. 5, completing the five-year upgrade.

items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) says the strong El Niño developing in the tropical Pacific is expected to peak in December and is nearly certain to persist until February 2027. The climate pattern, which warms the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, is forecast to bring above-average temperatures across much of the world and shift rainfall patterns, increasing drought and flood risks in different regions. In Ecuador, the Navy’s Oceanographic and Antarctic Institute reported sea temperatures as much as 5.2°C above normal off Ecuador and Peru. It linked the unusually warm water to exceptional coastal rainfall, rainfall deficits in the Andean highlands and Amazon, and reduced nutrient levels affecting some fisheries. Officials urged preparations for coastal flooding. Separately, Copernicus reported that the global average sea-surface temperature outside polar regions reached a September record of 21.05°C.

Record October tides flooded roads, homes and businesses along California’s coast this week, prompting warnings that storms during El Niño could worsen flooding. In Marin County, drivers were rescued from flooded cars and kayakers crossed streets; in Newport Beach, flooding blocked access to a local boat company’s dock. items.title: [dagenslantbruk.se] Swedish survey finds valuable meadows stable, but upkeep remains essential
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Sweden’s valuable meadows and grazing lands have largely retained their natural and cultural value, according to an analysis by the Swedish Board of Agriculture. Of 300,000 hectares identified as valuable, 260,000 had been fully inventoried. In 2020, nearly 70% of that fully inventoried area — 175,000 hectares — received environmental management payments, 8,000 hectares more than in 2018. Repeat surveys conducted 10 to 20 years apart found that most inventoried sites remained meadows or pastures. Some sites lost value when left unmanaged and became overgrown, while restoration helped recover value elsewhere. The agency says continued inventories are needed to track changes.

items.title: [independent.co.uk] Climate tracker projects 857,000 heat deaths as Super El Niño intensifies
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

A University of Chicago Climate Impact Lab tracker projects about 857,400 additional heat-related deaths worldwide from June 2026 through March 2027 as a Super El Niño develops. It estimates 484,500 excess deaths from June through September and forecasts another 372,900 over the next six months. The projected toll rose after August and September were warmer than the lab had forecast. The figures are model estimates, not confirmed death counts. The tracker projects the highest additional death tolls in India, Nigeria and China over the full period, with Nigeria forecast to have the most deaths in the next six months. Sea temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific’s Niño 3.4 region were 3.4°C above usual levels during Oct. 18-24, and the World Meteorological Organization expects the event to become much stronger than a typical El Niño between November and January. Health experts warn that women and girls may spend more time collecting water and providing care during extreme heat, while unreliable electricity and unsafe housing can make heat advice difficult to follow.

items.title: [LoRaMeshDevices] This Tiny Meshtastic Node Is Solar Ready: Base Uno First Look
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The Muzi Works Base Uno caught my attention because it packs quite a few useful features into a very small Meshtastic board. It comes pre-flashed, includes a 1,500 mAh battery, and has dedicated connections for a solar panel. That is a pretty interesting starting point for a little off-grid node. I bought the kit to find out how easily it would get going and whether the solar input actually worked. By the end of my first round of testing, it had connected over Bluetooth, discovered nearby nodes, completed a traceroute, and charged its battery to around 96% using a small solar panel. So far, this little board is looking good. Key Takeaways The Base Uno kit includes a pre-flashed Meshtastic board, antenna, and 1,500 mAh three-wire LiPo battery. Bluetooth pairing worked with PIN 123456, and I retained Long Fast to match my existing mesh. A small solar panel connected to PV+ and ground raised the reported battery level to about 96%. The app eventually showed 33 online nodes, and a traceroute to a node roughly a mile away succeeded. Table of Contents What Comes in the Base Uno Kit? The Three-Wire Battery Is an Interesting Detail Hardware Connections for Expansion and Solar First Power-Up and Bluetooth Pairing Configuring LoRa to Match the Local Mesh Node Discovery Took a Little Patience Connecting a Small Solar Panel More Nodes and a Successful Traceroute A Mobile Node or a Permanent Solar Node? What Comes in the Base Uno Kit? The kit includes the essentials for getting the board powered up and connected: The Base Uno board, carrying Elecrow and Muzi Works branding. A small screw-on antenna. A USB cable. A 1,500 mAh rechargeable LiPo battery. A small Allen key and screws. The board itself is quite compact. There is a reset button and a user button, but no display. Configuration and status checks happen through the Meshtastic app rather than on a screen attached to the node. Its nRF processor is one reason I was interested in it. This is the sort of hardware I would expect to be light on battery use, which makes it appealing for both a portable device and a solar-powered installation. I have not measured its power consumption or battery runtime yet, though, so those remain things to test rather than results from this first look. The Three-Wire Battery Is an Interesting Detail The included battery stood out more than I expected. It is a 1,500 mAh LiPo with three wires, rather than just the usual positive and negative leads. The third wire is a sensing connection. My understanding is that it provides battery temperature information that the charging circuitry can use to manage charging, including stopping it when conditions are unsuitable. That is particularly interesting on a board intended for solar use. I like seeing that extra sensing connection, but I did not test the temperature cutoff or establish its operating thresholds. The important distinction here is that the battery offers more than a simple two-wire power connection. Confirming exactly how the board responds to that sensing input will need further testing. Hardware Connections for Expansion and Solar There is quite a bit available around the edges of this little board: QWIIC port: An expansion connection I plan to try in a separate test. SDA and SCL pins: The labeled I2C connections. TX and RX pins: Serial connections for additional projects. OLED-related connections: Useful options if a display becomes part of the build. PV+ and ground: The dedicated solar-panel connections. Battery connector: Located on the back of the board, separate from the QWIIC port. That last distinction is worth paying attention to during assembly. The battery does not plug into the QWIIC port. I checked the connector location and orientation before seating it in the battery socket on the back. The PV+ and ground connections are what make this especially tempting as a solar-node project. Rather than starting with a separate charging arrangement, there is already a place on the board to bring in the panel. First Power-Up and Bluetooth Pairing Connect the antenna before powering up the node. I screwed on the supplied antenna first, then connected the battery. An LED came on straight away, which was a good start. The package identified the board as pre-flashed with Meshtastic, so there was no initial firmware installation to work through. My setup sequence was straightforward: Attach the antenna. Plug the battery into the correct battery connector. Open the Meshtastic app and look for the node over Bluetooth. Select the discovered Meshtastic device. Enter the Bluetooth pairing PIN. Allow the app to load the node information. Because there is no display, I tried the default PIN, 123456, and it connected successfully. The Bluetooth settings later confirmed that this was the configured PIN. It can be changed there rather than left at the default. My unit arrived running Meshtastic 2.7.15. The app initially reported the battery at 45%, while a later device-metrics reading showed 67%. Those were the reported values during setup, not a controlled battery-capacity measurement. Changing the Node Name I went into the user settings and gave the node a recognizable name using my vervesoft.live naming scheme with a Muzi identifier. Saving the change caused the node to reboot. The Bluetooth connection dropped while it restarted, and the status LED changed colors before the node returned. The same behavior occurred when saving the LoRa settings. A brief disconnect after saving was part of the restart, not a failed setup. Configuring LoRa to Match the Local Mesh The board initially had the Long Fast modem preset selected. My other nodes were still using Long Fast, so I kept this board on the same settings for the first test. Selecting the US region in the app changed the preset to Long Turbo during this setup. I changed it back to Long Fast so the Base Uno would match my existing nodes. These were the US-region combinations shown during the test: Long Fast: Frequency slot 20, operating at 906.875 MHz. Long Turbo: Frequency slot 14, operating at 908.75 MHz. Long Turbo was the newer default I encountered at the time, but compatibility with the mesh I already had running was the immediate priority. There was no point leaving this one node on a different preset while the rest were still waiting to be migrated. Choose the correct region for your location and check that the radio settings match the nodes you intend to use. The US settings above describe this particular setup, not a configuration to copy regardless of country. Other Settings I Checked With the radio configured, I worked through the remaining settings: Channels: A Long Fast channel was already present. Position sharing: The installed firmware allowed it on that channel, with an approximately 1.8-mile position-precision radius shown. Device role: The board was set to Client. Time zone: I used the computer’s time zone. Buzzer: The configuration listed pin 22, although I did not add or test a buzzer. Display: Display settings were turned off. Bluetooth: The fixed PIN was set to 123456. There was no GPS installed on this setup, so the position-sharing option did not mean the board was producing its own GPS location. It also had no environmental readings available. Node Discovery Took a Little Patience At first, the node list stayed empty apart from the Base Uno itself. I enabled the option to include unknown nodes, but there was still nothing else immediately. I expected it to find somebody fairly quickly. Instead of changing everything at once, I left it running and checked a few diagnostics. The signal-quality page did not provide a noise-floor reading with the installed firmware. It did show transmit and receive counters, including one TX and one RX at that stage. Battery telemetry was available, but there was no environmental or position data. Then another node appeared, identified as 49D4. That was the first useful confirmation that the Base Uno was receiving another mesh node. More entries followed as it continued running. The practical lesson from this first startup was simple: an empty node list in the first few minutes did not turn out to mean the board was faulty. In this case, it needed a little time. I also checked the firmware version against the releases available at the time. The unit had 2.7.15, while 2.7.26 was listed as the latest stable release then. I left the firmware alone for this test so I could establish how the kit behaved as supplied. Connecting a Small Solar Panel Once the basic setup was working, I tried the feature that interested me most: solar charging. I took a small panel described as roughly 200 mA and soldered its leads to the PV+ and ground connections on the back of the board. The LiPo battery remained connected, and I placed the assembly outside for a short test. The first solar test used a small panel connected directly to the board’s dedicated solar input. This was a bare-board experiment, not a finished outdoor installation. I still need to find a suitable case before turning it into a permanent node. Solar Charging Results There was a useful amount of sun, followed by some cloud, so the panel did not have uninterrupted sunshine throughout the test. Even so, the reported battery level rose from readings in the 60% to 70% range earlier in the session to approximately 95% to 96%. The device-metrics graph showed the upward charging trend after the assembly had been outside. That is the encouraging result: the solar input worked, and the reported battery charge increased while the node was operating. This was not a measured charging-efficiency test, and it does not yet establish whether this particular panel can sustain the node through nights and poor weather. It does show that the basic solar-charging arrangement is functional. More Nodes and a Successful Traceroute After the board had been running outside for a while, the app showed 33 online nodes with unknown entries filtered out. That was quite a change from the nearly empty list during the first few minutes. I then requested a traceroute to another node, and it returned successfully. The other node was roughly a mile down the road, which was a pleasing result with the little supplied stubby antenna still attached. I would not turn that into a maximum-range claim. This was an initial connectivity check, not a controlled range test. Still, the board was doing the things I wanted to establish first: receiving mesh traffic and completing a traceroute. A Mobile Node or a Permanent Solar Node? That is now the interesting decision. The Base Uno is small enough to make a neat portable build, but the dedicated solar input makes a permanent solar node very tempting. For a mobile build, the compact board and included 1,500 mAh battery are appealing. For a solar build, the working panel input and three-wire battery sensing are the details that stand out. My next steps are to find a case, update the firmware, and test the QWIIC port. I also want more time with the power system before making any claims about long-term autonomy. For now, this is a very positive first impression. It booted, paired, accepted configuration changes, discovered nearby nodes, and charged from a small solar panel. That is a pretty good start for a tiny Meshtastic board. Affiliate disclosure: I may earn from qualifying purchases through the product link below. items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Livestock guidance published across the United States, France and Poland focuses on forage stocks, grazing and feed transitions during drought and uneven feed supplies. In France, independent livestock nutrition consultant Eva Garre urged farmers to measure silage and hay reserves, account for losses of 15% to 30% and calculate shortages by date; early maize samples showed starch levels of 18 to 20 points, compared with the usual 34 to 37 in her region. Kenny Simon, an extension forages instructor at the University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture, recommended rotational grazing, moving hay-feeding sites and planting winter annuals to reduce stress on dry pastures. A Polish cattle farm keeps cows and calves on about 100 hectares of pasture from May through November and produces its own hay and silage. South Dakota State University Extension feedlot specialist Warren Rusche advised keeping newly arrived calves in smaller feedlot pens for their first three weeks and feeding them twice daily during the initial adjustment. Argentine feedlot analyst Andrés Halle cautioned that theoretical feedlot margins can misstate results when current grain prices are applied to grain produced on-farm.

items.title: [space.com] Mars orbiter detects volcanic gas above Alba Mons fissures
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The European Space Agency’s ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter has detected hydrogen chloride above fissures near Alba Mons, a vast Martian volcano, in a pattern researchers say may indicate gas escaping from magma beneath the surface. The gas appeared at a location and during a season that atmospheric models could not explain, and images show narrow fractures nearby. The study, published in Science Advances, identifies a possible volcanic origin but does not confirm an eruption. Researchers propose that the fractures connect to underground magmatic sources. Ice may seal them in winter, then sublimate as temperatures rise, allowing trapped gas to escape. The orbiter observed recurring, localized signals over four Earth years of targeted measurements. Atmospheric processes and surface storage could also explain the gas, and no new lava flow or eruption has been directly observed. If magma heats subsurface water, it could create hydrothermal environments of interest in the search for microbial life, but the study found no evidence of life itself. Researchers say further observations, including over the Tharsis and Cerberus regions, could test whether similar gas emissions occur elsewhere.

items.title: [sciencealert.com] Astronomers say ED138's dwarf-planet status awaits size measurements
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Astronomers say 2026 ED138, an icy object beyond Pluto and a potential dwarf planet, cannot be classified until researchers measure its size more accurately. Its estimated diameter ranges from 600 to 1,500 kilometers, and Matthew Holman, an astrophysicist at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, said the measurements may take months. The uncertainty arises because astronomers infer size from reflected sunlight: a small, bright object can appear as luminous as a larger, darker one. Infrared observations and longer-wavelength measurements with facilities such as Chile’s Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) could help narrow the size estimate; ALMA can detect light emitted by the object itself. If the body is large enough for its gravity to make it nearly round, it could qualify as the sixth dwarf planet recognized by the International Astronomical Union; the current size estimate alone does not establish its shape or status. Further observations will refine its size estimate, leaving astronomers and the Union to determine its classification.

Prime Minister Mark Carney is scheduled to meet Chinese leader Xi Jinping at the APEC summit in Shenzhen on Nov. 18-19.

items.title: [phys.org] Extra schooling under UK reform linked to fewer dementia diagnoses
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

A study of more than 100,000 UK Biobank participants found that a 1972 British law requiring teenagers to stay in school until 16 was associated with fewer diagnoses of Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias nearly 50 years later. Using the reform’s September 1, 1957, birth-date cutoff, researchers compared people subject to different school-leaving rules and reported a 0.88% reduction in dementia incidence among those affected. Researchers also found the reduction among participants with high genetic susceptibility. They cautioned that dementia was uncommon in this cohort, whose diagnoses were tracked only through age 65, making the estimate imprecise. Continued follow-up will help determine whether the difference persists as participants age.
